---
title: Token reference
description: What a theme actually needs to set, then every token and key in full.
icon: Table
---

A theme has three levels: **base tokens** (required), a **palette** (optional), and **theme keys** (optional).

Every theme key resolves in the same order:

1. The value you set in `keys`.
2. The palette entry the key derives from, if the key has one and you set it.
3. The base token the key derives from, if the key has one.
4. An Atlas default for the active appearance.

Each arrow below is the step failing. The first stop that has an answer is the one Atlas uses.

<Mermaid chart={`
flowchart LR
    K["a theme key"] -->|"not in keys"| P["palette entry"]
    P -->|"no palette source"| B["base token"]
    B -->|"no base source"| D["Atlas default"]
`} />

A key that derives its color is often transformed on the way: given a transparency, or mixed toward the background or the foreground. Those transforms apply only while deriving. A value you write in `keys` is used exactly as written.

## Start here

There are 73 theme keys, and a theme does not need most of them.

The 15 built-in themes set 34 of the 73 between them, and 30 of those appear in every one. None of them sets a single terminal, status, search, or agent key, because the palette already gets those right.

<Mermaid chart={`
flowchart LR
    subgraph A["73 theme keys"]
        subgraph B["34 set by some built-in theme"]
            C["30 set by all 15"]
        end
    end
`} />

So the realistic shape of a theme is:

1. **The 45 base tokens.** Required, and on their own they are a complete theme.
2. **The eight palette hues.** Eight lines that fix syntax, terminal, diff, status, and search colors at once.
3. **About thirty-five theme keys**, listed under [the working set](#the-working-set) below. These are the surfaces where a theme's own judgment genuinely differs from its base tokens: the syntax roles, the editor's own chrome, two borders, two panel surfaces, and the diff tints.

Everything below that is the long tail. Reach into it when a derived color is not the one you wanted, not as a checklist.

## Base tokens

All 45 are required in every variant. Leave one out and the file will not load. The names are shadcn/ui's, unchanged.

### Surfaces and text

| Token | Colors |
|---|---|
| `background`, `foreground` | the app background and default text |
| `card`, `card-foreground` | elevated panels |
| `popover`, `popover-foreground` | menus, popovers, and overlay panels |
| `primary`, `primary-foreground` | the signature color: selection tints, the brand fill and its hover state |
| `secondary`, `secondary-foreground` | secondary surfaces and their text |
| `muted`, `muted-foreground` | muted surfaces, dimmed text, comments, line numbers, ANSI bright black |
| `accent`, `accent-foreground` | the shadcn hover surface, and the matching-bracket fill |
| `destructive`, `destructive-foreground` | destructive actions, and the fallback for the error color |
| `border` | separators and control borders, and the source for the strong border |
| `input` | input borders |
| `ring` | the keyboard focus ring, and the matching-bracket outline |
| `chart-1` … `chart-5` | chart series. Five series, so keep them tellable apart: two that differ only slightly render as one line |
| `sidebar`, `sidebar-foreground` | panel and rail backgrounds, and their text |
| `sidebar-primary`, `sidebar-primary-foreground` | the signature color inside a panel |
| `sidebar-accent`, `sidebar-accent-foreground` | a panel's hover surface |
| `sidebar-border` | low-emphasis separators |
| `sidebar-ring` | focus inside a panel |

### Radius, type, and elevation

| Token | Notes |
|---|---|
| `radius` | the whole radius scale derives from it: controls at `radius − 4`, cards at `radius − 2`, popovers at `radius`, dialogs at `radius + 4`. Use a pixel value. The built-in themes all use `8px`. |
| `font-sans` | the interface font stack |
| `font-mono` | the editor, terminal, and code font stack |
| `font-serif` | required by the shadcn set; Atlas has no serif surface |
| `tracking-normal` | required by the shadcn set; Atlas does not currently read it |
| `spacing` | Atlas's density is built on the default `0.25rem`, which every built-in theme uses |
| `shadow-sm` | the raised elevation |
| `shadow-xl`, `shadow-2xl` | `shadow-2xl` is the menu and popover elevation; a dialog stacks `shadow-xl` beneath it |
| `shadow-2xs`, `shadow-xs`, `shadow-md`, `shadow-lg` | required by the shadcn set; Atlas renders three elevations and does not use these four |

<Callout type="info">
  Give a light variant its own shadow values. Dark shadows copied across read as heavy halos on a pale background.
</Callout>

## Palette

Eight optional hues. Each one is the first source for a group of theme keys, so setting the palette is the cheapest way to make syntax, terminal, diff, status, and search colors belong to your theme.

| Hue | Feeds |
|---|---|
| `red` | error status, ANSI red and bright red, the diff removal family, `syntax.tag`, `syntax.regexp` |
| `orange` | `syntax.number`, `syntax.constant` |
| `yellow` | warning status, ANSI yellow and bright yellow, `syntax.attribute`, both search-match highlights |
| `green` | success status and the live-capture indicator, ANSI green and bright green, the diff addition family, `syntax.string` |
| `cyan` | ANSI cyan and bright cyan, `syntax.type`, `syntax.operator`, `syntax.property` |
| `blue` | informational status, ANSI blue and bright blue, `syntax.function` |
| `purple` | ANSI magenta and bright magenta, `syntax.keyword` |
| `pink` | `syntax.escape` |

Set as many or as few as you like. Each entry is looked up on its own.

The names are hues, and everything downstream trusts them. A `green` holding your theme's cyan puts that cyan into ANSI green, added lines, and every success message at once.

## The working set

These are the keys to reach for first, and very nearly the set the built-in themes use: 34 of the 36 below appear in at least one built-in, the exceptions being the two diff text colors. The **Falls back to** column is what Atlas uses when you do not set the key.

### Syntax

Fifteen roles. They color code everywhere it appears: the editor, diffs, chat, and rendered markdown. This is where a theme's personality lives, and it is the one family worth setting by hand even when the palette is already right.

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `syntax.comment` | comments and prose quotes | base `muted-foreground` |
| `syntax.keyword` | keywords and control flow | palette `purple` |
| `syntax.string` | strings | palette `green` |
| `syntax.number` | numbers | palette `orange` |
| `syntax.type` | types, classes, and namespaces | palette `cyan` |
| `syntax.function` | functions and headings | palette `blue`, then base `primary` |
| `syntax.variable` | variables | base `foreground` |
| `syntax.operator` | operators | palette `cyan` |
| `syntax.tag` | markup tags | palette `red` |
| `syntax.attribute` | markup attributes, pragmas, and metadata | palette `yellow` |
| `syntax.constant` | constants, atoms, and booleans | palette `orange` |
| `syntax.regexp` | regular expressions | palette `red` |
| `syntax.escape` | escape sequences | palette `pink` |
| `syntax.definition` | definitions and strong prose | base `foreground` |
| `syntax.property` | properties and object keys | palette `cyan` |

### Editor

Ten keys. Worth setting when the editor surface is meant to differ from the app around it, which is common: Rosé Pine's editor background is a shade off its app background, and that difference is the whole reason this family exists.

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `editor.background` | the code editor background | base `background` |
| `editor.foreground` | default code text | base `foreground` |
| `editor.caret` | the caret | base `foreground` |
| `editor.gutter.background` | the gutter | base `background` |
| `editor.gutter.foreground` | line numbers | base `muted-foreground` |
| `editor.active_line.background` | the active line | base `foreground` at 4% |
| `editor.active_line.gutter_foreground` | the active line number | base `foreground` |
| `editor.selection.background` | selected code | base `primary` at 24% |
| `editor.match_bracket.background` | matching bracket fill | base `accent` |
| `editor.match_bracket.border` | matching bracket outline | base `ring` |

### Borders and panel surfaces

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `border.subtle` | low-emphasis separator | base `sidebar-border` |
| `border.strong` | high-emphasis border, including a focused control's | base `border` |
| `panel.background` | panel and rail background | base `sidebar` |
| `panel.input.background` | an input inside a panel | base `background` |

<Callout type="info">
  `border.strong` comes from `border`, not from `ring`. The focus ring is a brand color in most themes, and the strongest border is a gray one. A focused control's border is `border.strong` rather than a key of its own.
</Callout>

### Diffs

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `diff.added.background` | an added line or hunk | palette `green` at 13% |
| `diff.added.emphasis` | the changed words inside an added line | palette `green` at 34% |
| `diff.added.text` | added text, and the `+N` line count | palette `green` |
| `diff.removed.background` | a removed line or hunk | palette `red` at 13% |
| `diff.removed.emphasis` | the changed words inside a removed line | palette `red` at 34% |
| `diff.removed.text` | removed text, and the `-N` line count | palette `red` |
| `diff.context.background` | unchanged context | base `background` |

One fill serves both diff renderers, so a color you set here applies to the inline view and the side-by-side view alike.

## The rest of the key set

The other 37 keys. Every one of them derives correctly from a good palette and a good set of base tokens, which is why no built-in theme sets any of them. Set one when a derived color is specifically not what you wanted.

### Terminal

All nineteen. The bright ramp is the theme's hue pulled 15% toward the foreground, which reads as brighter in both appearances. Terminal authors who care about the exact ANSI ramp will want to set these; nobody else needs to.

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `terminal.background` | the terminal background | base `background` |
| `terminal.foreground` | default terminal text | base `foreground` |
| `terminal.cursor` | the cursor | base `foreground` |
| `terminal.ansi.black` | ANSI black | base `background`, 12% toward the foreground |
| `terminal.ansi.red` | ANSI red | palette `red` |
| `terminal.ansi.green` | ANSI green | palette `green` |
| `terminal.ansi.yellow` | ANSI yellow | palette `yellow` |
| `terminal.ansi.blue` | ANSI blue | palette `blue` |
| `terminal.ansi.magenta` | ANSI magenta | palette `purple` |
| `terminal.ansi.cyan` | ANSI cyan | palette `cyan` |
| `terminal.ansi.white` | ANSI white | base `foreground` |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_black` | ANSI bright black | base `muted-foreground` |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_red` | ANSI bright red | palette `red`, toward the foreground |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_green` | ANSI bright green | palette `green`, toward the foreground |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_yellow` | ANSI bright yellow | palette `yellow`, toward the foreground |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_blue` | ANSI bright blue | palette `blue`, toward the foreground |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_magenta` | ANSI bright magenta | palette `purple`, toward the foreground |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_cyan` | ANSI bright cyan | palette `cyan`, toward the foreground |
| `terminal.ansi.bright_white` | ANSI bright white | base `foreground`, lightened |

### Status

Four foregrounds. The tinted fill behind each one is not a key. See [what a theme cannot set](#what-a-theme-cannot-set).

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `status.success.foreground` | success text and icons, and the live-capture indicator | palette `green` |
| `status.warning.foreground` | warning text and icons | palette `yellow` |
| `status.error.foreground` | error text and icons | palette `red`, then base `destructive` |
| `status.info.foreground` | informational text and icons | palette `blue` |

### Interactive states and overlays

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `element.hover` | hover overlay on an element | base `foreground` at 4% |
| `element.selected` | selected overlay | base `foreground` at 6% |
| `element.active` | pressed overlay | base `foreground` at 8% |
| `element.highlight` | the 1px top edge on a raised surface | base `foreground` at 6% |
| `primary.hover` | hovered brand fill | base `primary`, 15% toward the foreground |
| `primary.muted` | muted brand fill | base `primary` at 6% |
| `selection.background` | document text selection | base `primary` at 18% |

These derive from the theme's own foreground, so they invert correctly between a dark and a light variant. A hardcoded white wash would not.

### Text, search, scrollbars, and the agent chip

| Key | Colors | Falls back to |
|---|---|---|
| `text.disabled` | disabled and unavailable text | base `muted-foreground`, 20% toward the background |
| `search.match.background` | a search match in the document | palette `yellow` at 22% |
| `search.match.active_background` | the match the cursor is on | palette `yellow` at 50% |
| `scrollbar.thumb.background` | scrollbar thumb | base `foreground` at 16% |
| `scrollbar.thumb.hover` | hovered scrollbar thumb | base `foreground` at 26% |
| `agent.chip.foreground` | agent identity chip text | base `foreground` |
| `agent.chip.background` | agent identity chip fill | base `foreground` at 6% |

<Callout type="info">
  There is one agent chip, not one per vendor. Atlas discovers the agents you have installed at runtime, so a theme cannot enumerate them, and no agent gets a color the others do not. This neutral pair is what a monochrome theme sets to flatten the chip entirely.
</Callout>

## What a theme cannot set

Six colors reach the app as `--atlas-*` custom properties but are not theme keys. Each is a pure function of a key that is, so writing one in a theme file is an unknown-key warning rather than an override.

| Variable | Derived from | How |
|---|---|---|
| `status.success.background` | `status.success.foreground` | that color at 12% |
| `status.warning.background` | `status.warning.foreground` | that color at 12% |
| `status.error.background` | `status.error.foreground` | that color at 12% |
| `status.info.background` | `status.info.foreground` | that color at 12% |
| `element.emphasis` | base `foreground` | at 16%: the strongest neutral overlay, such as a chat mention addressed to you |
| `terminal.selection` | base `primary` | at 30% |

The reason is that none of them is a judgment call. A status badge's fill is its status foreground at 12%, and an author who wants a different green wants a different green, not two greens that have to be kept in step. Change the key and the derived color follows.

## Where these end up

Atlas resolves the whole set on every theme change and writes it out as CSS custom properties. A base token becomes `--` plus its name, so `sidebar-border` is `--sidebar-border`. A theme key becomes `--atlas-` plus its name with dots and underscores turned into dashes, so `terminal.ansi.bright_red` is `--atlas-terminal-ansi-bright-red`. The six derived variables use the same `--atlas-` spelling.
